name: Fuyu persimmons
tile_uses: The halibut salad, mornings, a snack
why_now: Persimmons ripen on bare trees in November, and San Diego County grows them. Fuyus are the squat, tomato-shaped kind you can eat crisp like an apple — sweet, a little like honey and pumpkin.
how_to_choose: Squat and flat-bottomed: that's a Fuyu, ready to eat firm
Deep orange all over, with no yellow-green patches
Firm but not rock-hard for salads; a little give for eating out of hand
Skip pointed, acorn-shaped ones unless they're jelly-soft: those are Hachiya
buy_this_much: 4. Two for the salad beside the fish, two for mornings.
price_note: Sold by the each. Farmers markets often have them in bags for less.

flavor_paths.name: Raw and thin
flavor_paths.description: With fennel, lemon, and olive oil. The halibut's salad.

flavor_paths.name: With Parmesan
flavor_paths.description: Thin slices, shavings, black pepper — the way pears and cheese work.

flavor_paths.name: On yogurt
flavor_paths.description: Sliced, with satsuma zest and a pinch of salt.

weekday_uses: Shaved into the salad beside seared halibut
Sliced over yogurt in the morning
With Parmesan and pepper, as a snack
weekend_use: On buttered toast with flaky salt, for a slow breakfast.
storage: On the counter until they're as soft as you like, then the fridge for up to a week.
one_thing_to_learn: Shape tells you how to eat a persimmon. A squat Fuyu is never astringent and can be eaten crisp. A pointed Hachiya is full of tannin until it's completely soft, like a water balloon; bite one early and your mouth goes dry.
